definition: Argument technology is a sub-field of collective intelligence and artificial intelligence that focuses on applying computational techniques to the creation, identification, analysis, navigation, evaluation and visualisation of arguments and debates.
details: In the 1980s and 1990s, philosophical theories of arguments in general, and argumentation theory in particular, were leveraged to handle key computational challenges, such as modeling non-monotonic and defeasible reasoning and designing robust coordination protocols for multi-agent systems. At the same time, mechanisms for computing semantics of Argumentation frameworks were introduced as a way of providing a calculus of opposition for computing what it is reasonable to believe in the context of conflicting arguments. With these foundations in place, the area was kick-started by a workshop held in the Scottish Highlands in 2000, the result of which was a book coauthored by philosophers of argument, rhetoricians, legal scholars and AI researchers. Since then, the area has been supported by various dedicated events such as the International Workshop on Computational Models of Natural Argument (CMNA) which has run annually since 2001; the International Workshop on Argument in Multi Agent Systems (ArgMAS) annually since 2004; the Workshop on Argument Mining, annually since 2014, and the Conference on Computational Models of Argument (COMMA), biennially since 2006. explainer.lead: Argument technology gives computers ways to work with reasons, objections and debates rather than treating every statement as isolated. It helps people find arguments, see how they conflict, assess what is reasonable to believe and navigate the resulting debate.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a class deciding whether to postpone a picnic, with some students giving reasons to go ahead and others raising objections. Argument technology is like a computer-assisted map of that discussion: it connects each reason to its claim, shows disagreements and helps everyone inspect which positions still hold up. It does not simply count votes or declare whoever speaks last the winner.
tiers.practitioner: Practitioners represent arguments and their relationships, then apply argumentation-framework semantics or other computational methods to evaluate conflicting positions. The field also covers identifying arguments, mining them from debates, and building navigation and visualisation interfaces; multi-agent coordination and defeasible reasoning are established settings. A key pitfall is confusing a formally defensible position with a factually true one, since evaluation depends on the arguments and relationships supplied.
tiers.paperLevel: Argument technology applies computation to the creation, identification, analysis, navigation, evaluation and visualisation of arguments and debates. Argumentation-framework semantics provide a calculus of opposition for determining what is reasonable to believe under conflict, while philosophical argumentation theory informs non-monotonic and defeasible reasoning and multi-agent coordination. A workshop in the Scottish Highlands in 2000 helped consolidate the area, followed by dedicated meetings including CMNA, ArgMAS, COMMA and the Workshop on Argument Mining.

explainer.example: In a council debate, one argument says, "Close the bridge because its deck is unsafe," while another says, "Keep it open because the repairs are complete." The system records the opposition between them, evaluates which positions remain defensible under its chosen semantics, and displays the relationship so a user can inspect the reasoning instead of seeing only two isolated claims.

usedIn.detail: Models conclusions that can be withdrawn when a conflicting argument or exception appears.

usedIn.name: Multi-agent systems
usedIn.detail: Supports robust coordination protocols when agents hold competing positions.

usedIn.name: Debate analysis
usedIn.detail: Identifies and evaluates arguments, then presents their conflicts for navigation and visualisation.

usedIn.name: Argument mining
usedIn.detail: Applies computational techniques to finding arguments in natural discussion.

explainer.intuition: A debate is more than a pile of statements: claims are supported, challenged and sometimes defeated by other claims. Argument technology turns those relationships into something a computer can process and a person can inspect.
howItWorks: Collect or create claims and the reasons offered for them.
Identify arguments and represent their conflicts or opposition.
Analyse the structure and apply semantics to evaluate competing positions.
Present the results so users can navigate and visualise the debate.
explainer.whyItMatters: Conflicting reasons are central to deliberation, coordination and belief revision, but difficult to manage as debates grow. Argument technology supplies shared computational methods for evaluating opposition and making the structure of a debate visible.
misconceptions: It is not just vote counting: reasons and their conflicts are represented explicitly.
A defensible argument is not automatically a true statement about the world.
The field includes more than visualisation; it also covers identification, analysis and evaluation.
